title: Vienna, Bombay, London: the School Founded Three Times
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Vienna, the poet's daughter is born
stops.date_confidence: Attested: 18 October 1905, given by en.wikipedia and by the City of Vienna's own Wien Geschichte Wiki. No street address for the birth survives in any reachable record, so the pin is the city centre and the gap is stated rather than filled. Her father's death in 1908 is attested by de.wikipedia, which names him 'Alfred Sofer (Dichter, gestorben 1908)'.
stops.campa: Hilde Sofer is born in the imperial capital to Elise Sofer and to Alfred Sofer, a poet who dies before she is four. No street survives in the record; the city is the only address anyone can give her birth. The house that raises her is Jewish, bourgeois, musical, and the empire it belongs to has eleven years left to run. Of her father she keeps a shelf of verse and almost no memory of the man. She traces her own artistry to him anyway, in the pages she writes at the end of her life.
stops.quote: I barely remember him, but he left behind some beautiful poetry. I'm sure my sense of artistry comes from him.
stops.quote_source: Hilde Holger, autobiographical 'History Pages', quoted on the Hilde Holger Archive biography page (hildeholger.com)
suggested_refs: The surviving verse of Alfred Sofer, the only trace of him she could describe

stops.name: Poetzleinsdorfer Schlosspark, the moonlit dance
stops.date_confidence: Undated tradition. The estate's Vienna page tells this as a first-person memory with no year attached; 1918 is set only to order the segment. Note a correction: the research pool carried this episode as a 1926 sitting as nude model for a sculpture by 'Josef Heu'. The source says nothing of the kind. There is no sculpture, no modelling session and no 1926, and the sculptor is spelled Joseph Heu.
stops.campa: At six she is put to dance lessons. The district she grows up on the edge of is Vienna's green rim, vineyards and a park with a baroque house at the top of it, and nobody but Holger herself ever describes what happens there. In her own late pages she sets one scene above the others. A moonlit night, the sculptor Joseph Heu and a friend asking her to dance, and the girl taking her clothes off and dancing naked on the grass. She tells it as an origin rather than as a scandal.
suggested_refs: The Hilde Holger Archive 'History Pages', the only witness to the Poetzleinsdorf episode
sources: en.wikipedia, 'Hilde Holger' (dance training from about age six)

stops.name: Lothringerstrasse, the academy and Bodenwieser
stops.date_confidence: Year attested by en.wikipedia, METROMOD and the estate biography; month and day unknown and defaulted to 01-01. The story that Bodenwieser first advised Elise Sofer to withdraw her daughter is reconstruction, appearing in later biography and in no academy record.
stops.campa: Thirteen or fourteen years old, she enters Gertrud Bodenwieser's class at the imperial academy on Lothringerstrasse, and stays formed by it for the next eighty years. What Bodenwieser teaches is Ausdruckstanz, the expressive dance that Rudolf von Laban and Mary Wigman are building in Germany out of the same refusal of ballet's fixed vocabulary, and Holger will name them among her sources all her life. A later story has Bodenwieser telling her mother to take the girl away, too single-minded to be safe.
suggested_refs: Gertrud Bodenwieser's class at the k.k. Akademie fuer Musik und darstellende Kunst

stops.name: Vienna Secession, the first solo evening
stops.date_confidence: Year attested by en.wikipedia and by the estate's own Vienna performance register, which lists the Secession for 1923; the month and day are not given anywhere and are defaulted.
stops.campa: At eighteen she leaves the group and dances alone, in the building the Secessionists put their motto over. The programme is her own choreography: Schubert's Die Forelle, and Debussy's Le Martyre de Saint Sebastien. One dead Viennese and one living Frenchman, a folk song about a trout and a martyrdom, in a single evening. Neither dance is ever set down in notation, and she will still be able to stand up and demonstrate both of them sixty-nine years afterwards. The estate's Vienna register lists the Secession for 1923 and gives no month.
suggested_refs: The Secession building on Friedrichstrasse, venue of her independent debut

stops.name: Wiener Konzerthaus, dancing before Krishnamurti
stops.date_confidence: Undated and uncorroborated. Holger's own retrospective account places this in the 1920s; the estate confirms that a Theosophical Congress performance took place at the Konzerthaus, but no congress programme confirming Jiddu Krishnamurti's presence was located. The 1926 date orders the segment only.
stops.campa: A Theosophical Congress fills the Konzerthaus. Holger dances a Handel Largo with Gisa Geert, and in front of her, by her account alone, sits Jiddu Krishnamurti, the young Indian the Society has raised to be its World Teacher and who has not yet dissolved the order built around him. No congress programme has been found that puts him in the hall on a night when she was on the platform. Decades later she still names the evening, not for the dance but for who was watching it. Thirteen years afterwards she is living in his country.
suggested_refs: Programmes of the Vienna Theosophical Congress held at the Konzerthaus in the 1920s, not located

segments.name: Singerstrasse: The New School of the Art of Movement

stops.name: Singerstrasse, the school in the baroque palace
stops.date_confidence: Year attested by en.wikipedia and the estate biography; month and day unknown. The building is called the Palais Ratibor in the estate's literature and identified as the Palais Neupauer-Breuner in scholarship (Kampe 2013); both names are for the same house on Singerstrasse.
stops.campa: At twenty she leaves Bodenwieser's company and opens her own school in a baroque palace on Singerstrasse, under the city's protection. The estate calls the building the Palais Ratibor and scholars call it the Palais Neupauer-Breuner; it is the same house. She hires a faculty and sets them to teach the history of dance and music, art appreciation, costume and stage design, and anatomy, on the principle that a dancer who knows only steps is not an artist. Her own name for the place is the New School of the Art of Movement.
stops.quote: I called it the 'New School of the Art of Movement'. The curriculum included, history of dance and music, art appreciation, costume and stage design, anatomy.
stops.quote_source: Hilde Holger, autobiographical 'History Pages', quoted on hildeholger.com/vienna/
suggested_refs: The Palais Neupauer-Breuner, Singerstrasse, Vienna, seat of the Neue Schule fuer Bewegungskunst
sources: Thomas Kampe (2013), cited in the dossier

stops.name: Urania, the halls that were not theatres
stops.date_confidence: The estate's Vienna performance register lists the Urania for 1928, 1929 and 1935, and the Redoutensaal der Hofburg for 1929; the stop is dated to the first of these and months are not given. The register is a primary document held by the family.
stops.campa: The Urania on the Danube canal is an adult education house with an observatory dome on its roof, and Holger dances there in 1928, in 1929 and again in 1935. It is not a commercial theatre and its audience has not paid for fashion; it has come to be taught something. She works this circuit on purpose, the lecture halls and the exhibition rooms and the public parks. In 1929 the Redoutensaal of the Hofburg takes her company too, expressionist dance in a hall built for imperial masked balls.
suggested_refs: The Wiener Urania and the Redoutensaal der Hofburg, both listed in the estate's Vienna performance register

stops.name: Wiener Stadtpark, the children before the Strauss monument
stops.date_confidence: The estate register lists the Johann Strauss-Denkmal exactly once, for 1930; month and day are not given. Correction to the research pool, which gave this a 1926-1938 range: that range appears in no source and has been narrowed to the single attested year.
stops.campa: Her children's group performs in the Stadtpark at the foot of the gilded Johann Strauss, playing his violin inside a marble arch. She has them move to the spoken word and often to no music at all, so that they will not imitate the adult ballet they have watched. Passers-by stop on the gravel and are puzzled. Children on a Viennese stage in 1930 are expected to be miniature adults in costume, and these ones are not in costume and are not being miniature. She takes the music away, she says, because music tells a child in advance what to do.
stops.quote: I let children dance to music and to the spoken word, also to move without music. At that time people were not accustomed to see children moving naturally.
stops.quote_source: Hilde Holger, autobiographical 'History Pages', quoted on hildeholger.com/vienna/
suggested_refs: The Johann Strauss monument in the Wiener Stadtpark, listed for 1930 in the estate register
sources: hildeholger.com/vienna/ (her own account of the pedagogy)

stops.name: Zedlitzgasse, the Hagenbund and the orchid
stops.date_confidence: The estate register lists a Hagenbund exhibition, 'Der Tanz', for 1933; no month is given. The Ravel piece Orchid is described in Holger's own words on the estate's Vienna page. The programme title 'Colour and Line and Music' comes through the dossier's repertoire section.
stops.campa: The Hagenbund mounts an exhibition called Der Tanz in its hall on Zedlitzgasse, and Holger brings a programme she calls Colour and Line and Music, dance built to be looked at the way a painting is looked at. The year is 1933, and across the border the German schools that trained her own teachers are being emptied that season. Vienna is still arguing about whether dance belongs in an art gallery. In the gallery she dances Orchid, set to Ravel: a flower unfolding, opening and dying inside a few minutes of music.
suggested_refs: The Hagenbund exhibition 'Der Tanz', Zedlitzhalle, Vienna, 1933

stops.name: Waehringer Guertel, the massage certificate
stops.date_confidence: Undated. The dossier places the therapeutic massage training at the Rothschild-Spital somewhere in the 1930s and no source narrows it further; 1935 orders the segment only. The hospital's location is independently documented in Viennese Jewish institutional history; the training itself rests on estate and obituary material.
stops.campa: Somewhere in the 1930s, on a date no source will give, she trains in therapeutic massage at the Rothschild Hospital, the Jewish foundation on the Waehringer Guertel. It is a sensible second trade for a dancer, hands that already know where muscle attaches to bone. She is in her late twenties or her early thirties, the record not being exact enough to say which. In Bombay, four or five years later, with no engagements and no money, the massage pays for the room before the dancing pays for anything.
suggested_refs: The Rothschild-Spital on the Waehringer Guertel, Vienna's principal Jewish hospital
sources: dossier synthesis of estate and obituary material
standard Viennese Jewish-institutional history for the hospital site

stops.name: Singerstrasse, the school is closed
stops.date_confidence: Attested: en.wikipedia dates the Anschluss-related end of her Viennese career to 12 March 1938. That she went on teaching privately for a time is tradition, carried by the obituaries only. No individual Reich file naming her as a banned or degenerate artist was located.
stops.campa: The Anschluss arrives in March, and within weeks a Jewish woman may not work, may not perform, may not keep a school. The rooms on Singerstrasse are shut. She is thirty-two, at the height of a career built entirely in one city, and it ends inside a fortnight without a single document being issued in her name: no Reich file calling her a degenerate artist has ever been found, because none was needed. For a while, the tradition says, she goes on teaching in private rooms.
suggested_refs: The closure of Vienna's private Jewish-run schools and academies in the spring of 1938
sources: dossier synthesis of the Guardian and Independent obituaries

stops.name: Vienna, Canetti's dedication
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction, and a contradiction inside the research pool resolved downward. The chronology lens tagged this claim [R] and the geography lens tagged the identical event [A]. It rests on one estate-held book that no independent scholar is shown to have examined, so [R] stands. The month comes from the dossier; the day is unknown, and the place in the city is not recorded.
stops.campa: In July, weeks before she gets out, Elias Canetti inscribes a copy of Die Blendung to her. The novel is four years old and its author has not got out either. Nobody outside the family has been shown to have opened the book since, so the friendship rests on a flyleaf and nothing else, and where in the city he put it into her hands is not recorded anywhere. It leaves Austria in her luggage the following June, inscribed in herzlicher Freundschaft, in heartfelt friendship.
suggested_refs: The inscribed copy of Elias Canetti's Die Blendung in the Hilde Holger Archive, not independently examined
sources: dossier, citing the surviving dedication in the family archive

stops.name: Paris, the transit with the body luggage
stops.date_confidence: The June 1939 departure and the summer arrival in Bombay are attested by en.wikipedia and METROMOD. The Paris transit and the inventory of what she carried come from a German museum chronology cited in the dossier without naming the institution, so the routing is [R]. Correction to the pool: the friend who arranged the passage is Charles Petrach, spelled so by en.wikipedia, de.wikipedia and the estate alike. 'Karl Petrasch' appears in no source.
stops.campa: She leaves Austria in June and goes east by way of Paris, carrying costumes, photographs, scores and stage designs, the luggage of a body of work rather than of a household. A friend already in India, Charles Petrach, has arranged the passage at the last moment. She could have gone to the United States instead, and her stated reason for choosing Bombay is not safety but the pull the East has always had on Western artists. The dossier says elsewhere that Britain refused her entry. Nobody has reconciled the two accounts.
stops.quote: Having the choice of going to the United States or to India I chose the latter being a country of attraction to most Western artists
stops.quote_source: Hilde Holger, autobiographical 'History Pages', quoted on the Hilde Holger Archive biography page
suggested_refs: The trunk of costumes, scores and photographs carried out of Austria in June 1939, later the seed of the Hilde Holger Archive
sources: dossier, citing an unnamed German museum chronology

stops.name: Vienna, the family that stays
stops.date_confidence: Attested that her mother, her stepfather Heinrich Wohl and other relatives were murdered in the Holocaust (en.wikipedia). The date is not established anywhere and is set to the Vienna deportation window of 1941-42. Two corrections to the pool: it dated the murders to 1938, which is the Anschluss and not a deportation year, and it named a sister, who appears in no fetched source. The figure of fourteen relatives, from the Guardian obituary, is repeated everywhere and corroborated by no victim-by-victim record.
stops.campa: Her mother, her stepfather Heinrich Wohl and other relatives do not get out. They are murdered in the Holocaust, taken in the Viennese transports while she is teaching in Bombay. The obituaries settle on a number, fourteen relatives, and repeat it for sixty years; no list of the fourteen has ever been produced, and Holger herself gives no count in the pages she leaves. What she says instead, for the rest of her life, is that she was the one who was got out in time.
suggested_refs: The Vienna deportation lists of 1941-42, against which the figure of fourteen relatives has never been checked
sources: dossier, flagging the Guardian obituary's unverified figure

segments.name: Bombay: The School in Queen's Mansion

stops.name: Taj Mahal Palace Hotel, the first Indian engagement
stops.date_confidence: 1939, not 1941. The estate biography makes the Taj her first Indian performance, and METROMOD gives it as her first Indian venue after the summer 1939 arrival; the research pool's chronology lens dated it 1941 and contradicted its own geography lens. Month and day are unknown. The refusal to dance on the dinner floor comes from Krishna Lupus, 'A Heroine in Our Midst', BLITZ, 27 March 1948, a near-contemporary profile known only through the dossier, and is therefore [R].
stops.campa: Her first Indian engagement is a hotel bill: the Taj Cabaret, Teddy Weatherford's orchestra out of Chicago, and a Viennese modern dancer nobody in Bombay has heard of. She is asked to dance on the dinner floor, on parquet, among the tables. She refuses, and holds out until she is given a stage. The story comes back to her nine years later in a Bombay weekly as the evening the city learned what she was. She has been in the country a few weeks and she is thirty-three.
suggested_refs: Krishna Lupus, 'A Heroine in Our Midst', BLITZ, Bombay, 27 March 1948

stops.name: Bhopal, the piano carried seventy miles
stops.date_confidence: The estate biography names the Nawab of Bhopal outright and ties the invitation directly to the Taj performance. Correction to the pool, whose geography lens hedged between Bhopal and Akbar Hydari of Hyderabad and called the record unresolvable: Hyderabad appears in no fetchable source. The seventy-mile piano remains [R], and the date is unknown, set here only to follow the Taj engagement.
stops.campa: The Nawab of Bhopal, hearing about the hotel performance, invites her to the palace to dance. A dancer needs an accompanist and an accompanist needs an instrument, so a piano is carried seventy miles across country. Nobody but Holger records the piano or the distance, and no source gives the month or even the year with confidence. By her account the instrument reaches the palace barely playable, knocked out of tune by the road, and she dances to it as it is.
suggested_refs: The court of the Nawab of Bhopal, her first princely engagement in India

stops.name: Bombay, the marriage to Adi Boman-Behram
stops.date_confidence: Year attested by en.wikipedia; month, day and place within the city are not given, so a Bombay pin is used. The dossier's date of dissolution, 1963, is contested by derivative sources giving 1975, and neither is settled.
stops.campa: She marries Ardeshir Kavasji Boman-Behram, a Parsi physician everyone calls Adi. The Parsis are Bombay's other exiles, arrived from Persia more than a thousand years before and busy ever since building the city's hospitals and colleges, and the marriage puts her inside a network of institutions that will lend her rooms and supply her audiences. It is the second year of the war. No month, no day and no place in the city is recorded, and the sources disagree about when the marriage ends: 1963 by one account, 1975 by another.
suggested_refs: The Parsi institutional network of colonial Bombay, through which most of her early engagements ran

stops.name: Capitol Cinema, the stage she has to bring herself
stops.date_confidence: The estate's Bombay register lists the Capitol across 1939-1942 without exact dates; 1940 sits inside that range and orders the segment. Her complaint about bare cinema stages comes from her own 1946 article for a dance periodical, quoted in the dossier; the article itself was not fetched.
stops.campa: Between 1939 and 1942 she dances in Bombay's cinemas, and a cinema supplies a screen, a shallow platform and nothing else. She brings her own curtains, her own lighting, her own backcloth, and is the entire technical department as well as the soloist. Her account of those bare stages comes from an article she writes in 1946, which survives only in quotation; the article itself has not been found. The audience in front of her is Indian, British, Parsi and refugee at once, and most of it has never seen a European dance that was not ballet.
stops.quote: Against the greatest prejudice, ignorance and lack of background for Western art, I had to start my work and bring greater understanding and appreciation of Western art to the east.
stops.quote_source: Hilde Holger, autobiographical 'History Pages', quoted on the Hilde Holger Archive biography page
suggested_refs: Holger's 1946 article for the periodical Dance, on the bare stages of Bombay's cinemas

stops.name: Queen's Mansion, the School of Art for Modern Movement
stops.date_confidence: October 1941 attested by METROMOD, which also confirms the second floor and the school's own advertised description; Kampe supplies the same month. The day is unknown. Correction to the pool: its coordinate for Queen's Mansion was about 1.4 km north of the building, out past Masjid; the Fort address is used here.
stops.campa: On the second floor of Queen's Mansion on Prescott Road she opens the School of Art for Modern Movement, advertised as the foremost professional European school for creative dance and contemporary ballet in India. Admission is restricted to Ladies and Children, and the restriction is not modesty: a room in which women move for money can be read in this city as a brothel, and she writes plainly about what the word professional still means to the parents she has to persuade. Three and a half years after Vienna shut her rooms, she has a school again.
stops.quote: The word 'professional' had, till the last years, the same meaning as 'prostitution'
stops.quote_source: Hilde Holger, article for the periodical Dance, quoted on the Hilde Holger Archive biography page
suggested_refs: Queen's Mansion, Fort, Bombay, second floor: the School of Art for Modern Movement, opened October 1941
sources: Thomas Kampe, cited in the dossier

stops.name: Excelsior Theatre, Three Enchanting Ballets
stops.date_confidence: Both dates attested by the estate's Bombay register: '28 Feb & 4 Mar 1943, Excelsior, Bombay, 3 Enchanting Ballets'. Correction to the pool, which hedged the venue as 'Capitol/Excelsior': METROMOD's Capitol attribution is the outlier against the estate's own dated register, and the coordinate given for the Excelsior was about 880 m too far south.
stops.campa: On the twenty-eighth of February and again on the fourth of March she presents Three Enchanting Ballets at the Excelsior. The sets and costumes are by two painters: Magda Nachman, a Russian Jewish exile who reached Bombay by way of Berlin, and Shiavax Chavda, a Bombay artist trained in Paris and London. Three emigrations meet on one wartime bill. The estate's own register carries both dates and the venue; METROMOD puts the same programme at the Capitol instead, and no source explains the discrepancy.
suggested_refs: The stage designs of Magda Nachman and Shiavax Chavda for Three Enchanting Ballets, Excelsior, Bombay, 1943

stops.name: Bombay, the prayer meeting
stops.date_confidence: Undated. Holger's own Bombay pages describe attending Gandhi's daily prayer meetings and meeting him, and give no year; 1944 orders the segment only. No location within the city is named in the source, so a Bombay pin is used and the gap is stated.
stops.campa: Thousands come every day to Mohandas Gandhi's prayer meetings, and Holger comes too, takes her shoes off at the door and gives the Hindu greeting with her palms together. She is a European in a room that is deciding whether Europeans will go on governing the country. She calls the meeting the greatest event of her Indian years, above every stage she danced on in them, and the pages she leaves give it no date at all. At the end of each meeting money is collected for the poor of India.
stops.quote: My greatest event there was to meet Ghandi who held his daily prayer meetings attended by thousands of people, where he always collected money for the poor of India. Of course I took my shoes off, walked into the room and gave the greetings as of all Hindus.
stops.quote_source: Hilde Holger, autobiographical 'History Pages', quoted on hildeholger.com/bombay/ (her spelling of the name preserved)
suggested_refs: Gandhi's daily prayer meetings in Bombay during the war years

segments.name: Partition, and the Passage to England

stops.name: Bombay, the news reaches the dress rehearsal
stops.date_confidence: The assassination date is fixed; her presence at a dress rehearsal when the news arrived is attested by her own account on the estate's Bombay page. The theatre is not named in any source, so a Bombay pin is used. That the assassination and the Partition violence together decided her departure is given by en.wikipedia and METROMOD; the dossier's stronger version, resting on family sources, is [R].
stops.campa: She has just finished directing a dress rehearsal when a man runs into the theatre shouting that Gandhi is dead. The company is Indian and European together, and by her account the grief does not sort itself by nationality. Partition has already turned the country's streets over to killing. The thirtieth of January closes the argument for her: she has watched one country decide who belongs in it and does not intend to watch a second do the same. No source names the theatre she was standing in.
stops.quote: I was still in Bombay when Ghandi was assassinated. I had just directed a dress rehearsal on stage when somebody rushed into the theatre shouting 'Ghandiji is dead', and a dreadful sadness came over all of us, Indians and Europeans.
stops.quote_source: Hilde Holger, autobiographical 'History Pages', quoted on hildeholger.com/bombay/ (her spelling preserved)
suggested_refs: The Bombay of January 1948, between Partition and the assassination

stops.name: St Xavier's College Hall, the last Bombay performances
stops.date_confidence: Attested by the estate's Bombay register, which gives performances on 7-8 and 18 February 1948; the stop is dated to the first of them.
stops.campa: Nine years of work in the city end in a college hall in February, on the seventh and the eighth, then once more on the eighteenth. The estate's register gives those three dates and nothing about what was danced on them. She will not stand in Bombay again for thirty-five years. The school on Prescott Road has trained a generation of dancers who had nowhere else to learn what she taught, and it closes behind her when she goes. Some of the pupils keep teaching it. Indian dance schools still name her eighty years afterwards.
suggested_refs: The estate's Bombay performance register, 7-8 and 18 February 1948, St Xavier's College Hall
sources: metromod.net, 'Hilde Holger' (her Bombay period still taught in Indian dance schools)

stops.name: Ballard Pier, the second exile
stops.date_confidence: The 1948 departure for England is attested by en.wikipedia and METROMOD; the month is not established and is set to order the segment. The pier itself is an inference: no shipping manifest, ship's name or pier was located in any source, and Ballard Pier is offered only as the standard Bombay passenger port of the period. Their daughter Primavera was born in Bombay in 1946 (en.wikipedia, METROMOD).
stops.campa: Adi, Hilde and two-year-old Primavera sail for England. No manifest has been found and no ship's name; Ballard Pier is where Bombay's passengers boarded in those years and is offered as the likeliest quay rather than a documented one. She is forty-two, leaving her second country, with a husband, a daughter and the same trunk of costumes and photographs that came through Paris nine years before. The first departure was flight from people who wanted her dead. This one she chooses, having watched a country divided once already.
suggested_refs: Ballard Pier, Ballard Estate, Bombay: the passenger port of the period, offered as inference, not record

stops.name: Parliament Hill Fields, the third city
stops.date_confidence: That the family lived first in Hampstead before moving to Camden Town in 1951 is attested by the Islington Tribune. Correction to the pool, which cited hildeholger.com/biography/ for this: that page does not mention Hampstead at all and goes straight to the Camden basement. The Parliament Hill Fields specificity and the neighbours' suspicion of her accent are [R], uncorroborated. The school's name is 'Contemporary Dance', not 'Modern Dance', per en.wikipedia and the estate.
stops.campa: The family's first English address is on the edge of the heath. Postwar London hears a German-speaking accent and does not always trouble to distinguish the people who fled the Reich from the Reich; a later biographer records the neighbours' suspicion, and nothing contemporary corroborates it. Within the year she has founded the Hilde Holger School of Contemporary Dance, the third school she has opened on the third continent she has lived on. She is forty-three years old.
stops.quote: I have never been orthodox in my work and I welcome to my school anyone who is serious and unprejudiced.
stops.quote_source: Hilde Holger, autobiographical 'History Pages', quoted on the Hilde Holger Archive biography page
suggested_refs: The Hilde Holger School of Contemporary Dance, founded in Hampstead in 1948
sources: islingtontribune.co.uk, 'How dancer who fled Nazis found perfect stage in north London'

stops.name: Hampstead, Darius is born
stops.date_confidence: Year attested by en.wikipedia, which gives the Down syndrome and the heart and lung problems; month, day and hospital are not recorded anywhere, and the pin is the family's Hampstead address of that year. Both quoted lines, the doctor's and her own, come from her autobiographical pages as published by the estate.
stops.campa: Her son Darius is born in London with Down syndrome and with heart and lung trouble. No source records the hospital, the month or the day. The medical advice of 1949 is immediate and unanimous: you can put him in an institution, the doctor tells her, you must not keep him at home. It is the ordinary counsel of the period, given to every family in her position, and almost every family takes it. Nineteen years later the boy will dance in one of her own pieces on a public stage. She refuses, and keeps him.
stops.quote: I am his mother and brought him in this world and he will stay with me as long as I live.
stops.quote_source: Hilde Holger's reply to the doctor who advised institutionalising Darius, from her 'History Pages', quoted on hildeholger.com/london/
suggested_refs: British institutional practice for infants with Down syndrome in 1949, the advice she refused

stops.name: St Martin-in-the-Fields, Under the Sea
stops.date_confidence: Year attested by en.wikipedia and the estate's London page; month and day not given. Contradiction carried openly: an estate choreography list separately dates a Sadler's Wells presentation of the same work to 1955, and no source reconciles the two, so whether 1951 was a premiere or one item on a shared bill is unsettled.
stops.campa: She dances Under the Sea, set to Saint-Saens, on the altar steps of the church on Trafalgar Square, and London argues about whether a church may be used as a theatre. It is the performance that makes her name in England after three years of beginning again from nothing: a forty-five-year-old refugee with a school in a rented room, suddenly argued about. An estate list dates the same work to Sadler's Wells in 1955, and nobody has reconciled the two entries. Whether this evening was the premiere or one item on somebody else's bill, the record does not settle.
suggested_refs: Under the Sea, to Saint-Saens: the estate's competing 1951 and 1955 entries for the same work

stops.name: Oval Road, the basement
stops.date_confidence: The 1951 move to Camden Town is attested by the Islington Tribune; the month is not recorded. The fifty-year residency and basement studio are given by the estate biography. She lived here until 2001.
stops.campa: The family moves to Oval Road, between Primrose Hill and Regent's Park, and the basement becomes the studio. She teaches in it for fifty years: professional dancers, children, adults who have never danced, and people with disabilities in the same room on the same terms. No proscenium, no mirror wall, no company, no subsidy. What comes out of the basement across five decades reaches Sadler's Wells, the ICA and a Vienna stage. The room itself is under a house in Camden Town.
stops.quote: I do not want you to function as a machine
